For the first year of the project, we focussed a lot on a bottom-up theorem, that certain spaces of automorphic forms are finite-dimensional, and we are largely done with the proof. I have been quite bad at reviewing PRs recently (I'll get to why later on) but I had a go over the weekend and I've realised that we have done almost all of the adeles part of the argument and almost all of the finiteness part of the argument; what's left is some technical results about haar characters.

More recently I have turned to thinking about a top-down argument, which involves a lot of technical Galois representation stuff and modularity lifting theorems, and I've mostly been keeping myself to myself. I'm going to give 8 2-hour lectures at Imperial next term (Jan-March 2026) where I'm really going to push forwards with this stuff and actually write a blueprint; it has somehow taken me a very long time to flesh out the proof into something coherent which I understood all the details of, but I think I am there now modulo a modularity lifting theorem which is well-documented in the literature.

The thing that has been a big distraction for me recently is that I want to prove the main theorems of local class field theory and I've been working on this in private with a group of people who attended the Oxford Clay workshop on the topic. We have nearly finished the proof and this has become my main priority. I really hope to get back to bottom-up FLT soon and get the finiteness result sorry-free. I am naively hoping that I can get bottom-up FLT back on track and class field theory over the line by Christmas. Then in the new year I'm going to focus on top-down FLT.

There might be some money for jobs at Imperial, perhaps for people who are experts in the number theory related to top-down FLT and/or number theorists interested in AI. If there's anyone out there who would be able to move to Imperial quickly (e.g. by Jan) then could they let me know by DM? It's a pretty niche job description so I am not optimistic I'll find anyone appropriate but I thought I'd ask.

OK so here's a March update.

I am currently 6 lectures through an 8 lecture course on Fermat's Last Theorem (this is not a Lean course, it is a regular number theory graduate course), and I will be finished with this course on Thurs 26th March. Notes for the first 6 lectures are here https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/FLT/tree/main/2026_EPSRC_TCC_course . I had no idea how much work preparing this course would be and I have learnt a huge amount about the details of the proof which I'm proposing to formalize; teaching the course has forced me to understand many technical details of the argument. It has done me the world of good.

I did not/will not get as far as I had hoped; I wanted to prove all of "FLT modulo 1980s" but by now it's pretty clear that what I am going to end up proving is "FLT modulo 1980s and an automorphy lifting theorem" so I will give some lectures when Imperial's term starts again in late April which finish the job by proving the automorphy lifting theorem.

During the Easter break (i.e. starting in about 9 days) I will be writing up the proof of the finiteness theorem for the adeles which we spent most of last year formalizing. This will be a joint paper with other people and I feel like I want to be liberal with including people who contributed, so if you feel like you helped prove the finiteness theorem (e.g. if you contributed to the adeles miniproject, the Haar character miniproject or the Fujisaki miniproject) then let me know and we can figure out whether you end up as a coauthor or as someone who is heartily thanked.

After Easter I will give the remaining lectures on the automorphy lifting theorem (a generalisation of a modularity lifting theorem), and then we will have what could be described as a "pre-blueprint". It is a series of lecture notes which cover various mathematical arguments in great detail and assume various others but in essentially all cases with concrete references to the pre-1990 literature. My next task will be turning these notes into an actual blueprint. This blueprint will be slightly different to the usual blueprints because some notes will be marked as "known in 1980s" and so I will not be working on attempting to manually formalize these. However the main argument is something which I will continue to work on manually, not least because parts of it seem to me to be appropriate for mathlib.

Some of you will have seen Math Inc's announcement that I am now a Veritas Fellow. Math Inc are pushing the idea that I should not be focussing on FLT modulo 1980s but on all of FLT. Here are my thoughts on this huge extension to the FLT project.

Firstly, teaching the course has shown me exactly what the main bottlenecks are, and it seems to me that by far the hardest missing piece is Taylor's 1989 theorem attaching Galois representations to Hilbert modular forms (or more precisely to automorphic forms over a totally definite quaternion algebra over a totally real field; these are related to Hilbert modular forms via Jacquet-Langlands). Using Hilbert modular forms rather than classical modular forms makes a lot of arguments easier because it gives us an extra "degree of freedom" meaning that we can bypass many technical inputs (Ribet, Langlands--Tunnell) which Wiles needed. For example instead of level-loweing by proving delicate theorems about congruences between modular forms, we can just change the base field to change the level and use class field theory instead. Furthermore the automophy lifting theorem which we need is easier to prove for these totally definite quaternion algebra forms than for classical forms because there is no Shimura variety, it is just combinatorics. So there are many reasons why it's more desirable to work with this more general class of automorphic forms.

But the cost is that the "easy" direction of Langlands (they're both hard -- perhaps I mean "first, historically" direction), i.e., attaching Galois representations to Hilbert modular forms, is more technical than the classical work of Eichler and Shimura doing this for weight 2 modular forms forms. There are many hundreds of pages in this argument, when written out in full, and many complex definitions will be needed to formalize it (including all of global class field theory,Jacquet-Langlands, a careful analysis of the ell-adic cohomology of Shimura varieties etc). My mental model of what AI can do is constantly adjusting, but my mental model still says that this is way beyond what AI can do right now, and it is clearly a multi-year human project with many essential fundamental and complex definitions still missing from mathlib (and possibly a very long way from mathlib).

As a warm-up for that theorem one could also talk about Mazur's theorem, that every elliptic curve over Q has at most 16 torsion points. This is a 150 page paper of Mazur proved in 1978 and again my mental model says that formalizing this would be an extremely tall order. If and when we finish the 1990s part of FLT my instinct would be to move onto Mazur next because it is an incredibly beautiful piece of mathematics and again formalizing it would force us to formalize some fundamental mathematical objects (modular curves, Jacobians, Neron models etc) which would be good for the area in general. My mental model of what AI can do says that Mazur (150 pages, 1970s) is easier than Taylor (~1000 pages, 1980s). All known proofs of FLT use Mazur's theorem (applied to the Frey curve). Mazur's paper is here https://www.numdam.org/item/?id=PMIHES_1977__47__33_0 and the statement is here https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/FLT/blob/main/FLT/Assumptions/Mazur.lean -- it's just

import Mathlib.GroupTheory.Torsion
import Mathlib.AlgebraicGeometry.EllipticCurve.Affine.Point

open scoped WeierstrassCurve.Affine -- E⟮ℚ⟯ notation

theorem Mazur_statement (E : WeierstrassCurve ℚ) [E.IsElliptic] :
    (AddCommGroup.torsion E⟮ℚ⟯ : Set E⟮ℚ⟯).ncard ≤ 16 := sorry

Math Inc assure me that FLT is "one year away" and given that Taylor's result is probably 10x as hard as Mazur, Mazur's statement must be one month away, unless everything is very nonlinear (which it probably is).

Given Math Inc's interest in pushing full FLT over the line, I will (when I've finished writing the finiteness paper and finished giving my course proving the automorphy lifting theorem), as part of the exercise of writing a blueprint, be creating several more self-contained sorries corresponding to theorems proved in the 1980s or 1970s. I am currently tempted to put all of these statements in an FLT-AI repo positioned downstream from mathlib and upstream from FLT, where AI companies can attempt to autoformalize the papers, creating possibly poorly-written and hard-to-maintain code. I will continue to bump mathlib regularly on the FLT repo and when I do, I'll bump it on FLT-AI and if proofs break then hard luck. My job which I am currently paid to do is to formalize FLT modulo 1980s but things have moved on and perhaps the 1980s step will be done by AI. I am hoping that my AI challenges will be of interest to several AI companies, however I will almost certainly be continuing with the 1990s part of FLT as a human-written project (not least because ultimately large parts of it should be upstreamed to mathlib) and even if an AI company starts filling in sorries in this part of the project, I might well simply not merge them unless they are easy to review and tidy up.

I have no idea how realistic the prospect of getting full FLT over the line is, in the near future. What is clear is that progress in the 1980s part of the argument will almost certainly be AI-led autoformalization, at least in the near term. However I still fully believe that we are on track to get FLT modulo 1980s done by 2029 and hopefully earlier. What we do after that will depend on how good autoformalization has become.

I figured I should give an update to (my side of) the project to give people a sense of where the project is going so here it is.
As hinted by in Kevin’s blogpost and announced in the ZMC conference last week, I have now obtained a formal artifact of a modularity lifting theorem (depending on four axioms that are arguably known in the 80’s; details below) using Claude and Codex. The formal artifact consists of roughly 350k lines of unorganised and uncomprehensible AI slop, and is therefore useless and will not be public (yet).

The modularity lifting theorem is one of the two main post-80’s results that the proof being formalised will depend on, the other being Taylor’s residual potential modularity whose proof also depends on the modularity lifting theorem. Aside from these two, there are still work to be done, including stating all the pre-80’s results and also some hefty (but comparatively elementary) calculations to produce a formal artifact of FLT itself. But I would still say that a significant percentage of the work towards a formal artifact of FLT modulo 80’s is done. (I am not that familiar with the rest of the argument though and one would need to ask Kevin to get a more accurate estimation.)

That said, AFAIK the end goal of this FLT project is not merely to get a formal artifact of FLT. Since the proof of FLT is already checked by the union of generations of mathematicians, it is well accepted by the community to be correct, so such a formal artifact has no mathematical value aside from “being fun to have (per Kevin)”. The end goal, as I understand it, would be an actual formalisation of a nicely written exposition of the proof (See e.g. the verso blueprint).

So the next goal (of mine) would be to experiment on the formal artifact and try to turn it into a formalisation. I have some ideas to experiment with, and in the worst case scenario, 350k lines (which would probably translate to 100k+ lines of human code) is perhaps still in the magnitude that is feasible to a complete human rewrite. If anyone have ideas on how to turn this useless pile of junk into something useful (or maybe just curious to see how it looks), I am also happy to share parts of this artifact through DMs.

We say that a representation ρ:Gal⁡(F‾/F)→GL⁡2(A)\rho : \operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F) \to \operatorname{GL}_2(A)ρ:Gal(F/F)→GL2​(A) (where AAA is an O\mathcal{O}O-algebra) is modular of level SSS if there exists an O\mathcal{O}O-algebra homomorphism T(S)→A\mathbb{T}(S) \to AT(S)→A sending TvT_vTv​ to ρ(Frob⁡v)\rho(\operatorname{Frob}_v)ρ(Frobv​) for all v∉Sv \not\in Sv∈S.

And the four axioms are:

  • Local class field theory (whose statement is here which I tried (and failed) to get it into mathlib last year)
  • Existence of a modular Hecke-algebra valued Galois representation (whose hard part is attaching Galois representations to modular forms, and is arguably the hardest input to FLT)
  • The description of local flat deformation rings Rvfl≃O[[X4[Kv:Qp]−1]]R^{fl}_v \simeq \mathcal{O}[[X_{4[K_v:\mathbb{Q}_p]-1}]]Rvfl​≃O[[X4[Kv​:Qp​]−1​]] (which I might also nearly have a formal artifact for modulo Fontaine’s 264 page Asterisque book Groupes p-divisibles sur les corps locaux but it replaces this axiom with four axioms and it is harder to audit that they actually say the right things)
  • The formula on top of page 93 in Toby Gee's exposition with a missing -1 on the RHS added. This is basically Poitou-Tate + some mapping cone construction but it is quite hard to state the exact sequence (because one would need to construct all the maps) so I stated the required end result (computation of Euler characteristics) instead.
Congratulation! Even if you call it "AI slop" it's still an amazing achievement, and it's still interesting that the new proof is correct!

For sphere packing we first made Claude spend a few weeks cleaning up the code and that cut it in half. I expect something similar would happen here. Even more effective would be to make a Tau Ceti roadmap and add it there. I've seen the AI review process produce some much nicer code that the raw code you get from an AI.
Congrats ! And if “AI slop” is to be made of math , I would much rather it be someone from here who cares to do it for a good reason at least :star_struck:

I'd love to a Tau Ceti roadmap covering part or all of this. I've recently added a --source flag to the sample Tau Ceti worker, so once you have both a roadmap and relatively-cleaned-up repository, you can write

./tauceti work --loop --roadmap-only XXX --source YYY`

and your AI will identify material from YYY that contributes to roadmap XXX, and make PRs / respond to review comments.
